title: Granite is not useful
author: real_PommesPanzer
selftext:
Currently, I'm writing my own auto trader.

I tested IBM Granite 52-16 for time series prediction for stocks and options. Based on backtesting, the results were disappointing. If anyone has the same idea, you should not pursue it if you want to trade Top 40 Xetra and Top 50 S&P 500. I tested it against 5 year of data. 

Those were my results :

Direction: 48.6% and 48.5% against 55.8% and 56.0% up moves, so always guessing "up" would beat Granite by about 7 points.

Rank IC: -0.0011 and -0.0257, intervals include zero.

Gated vs random entries: validation +0.56% against random +0.54%, with a 95th percentile of +0.70%. The gate adds nothing.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Thanks for posting a clean negative result, those are rarer and more useful than the wins. And comparing against "always up" and random entries is exactly the right baseline. Most people skip both.

The random-entry check is the most convincing part: +0.56% vs +0.54%, with a 95th percentile of +0.70%, says the gate is noise very clearly.

One thing I'd add to close it out completely: the minimum effect your test could have detected. With rank IC intervals that include zero, it's worth knowing whether the interval was narrow (the model genuinely has nothing) or wide (the test couldn't have seen a small edge either way). Those are two different conclusions, and only the first one fully closes the idea.

My guess is it's the first. Generic time-series foundation models are trained on things like sales, weather and traffic, where the past really does predict the future. Stock returns are close to noise at short horizons, so the model ends up extrapolating patterns that aren't there.

replies.author: real_PommesPanzer
replies.body: Yeah that's was AIs first shot of suggestion for trading. But the conclusion that always up gives ~56% win rate was kinda funny. So basically just hope 7-day straight that the stock will win raise and you made plus. That's basically an ETF

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: Exactly. That’s why we keep working, looking for a strategy and digging for alpha. It’s hard work. Really hard work. We don’t get too excited or start hoping we’ll all be the next Elon Musks.

replies.author: real_PommesPanzer
replies.body: Stock market is not rational. A company with good fundamentals can plumit while struggling can raise. Next idea gather as much recent information as possible and fine tune rating

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Nothing is particularly rational these days. Trump says something and stocks go up. Then he says he changed his mind and they go down. Manipulation is everywhere — how are you supposed to find a rational edge in that? I don’t understand how people sell trading courses and claim they can teach you to trade. It’s basically the same as walking into a casino and putting it all on zero. It’s genuinely difficult. When I first started digging into this I thought it was nothing — we’d figure it out, no problem. Now I see it’s not nothing at all. It’s serious and hard. AI helps in the sense that it speeds things up and you don’t have to burn money while you test, but it’s still just a tool in human hands, at least for now.  
Tell me though — have you managed to find an edge yourself, or are you still searching like I am?

replies.author: real_PommesPanzer
replies.body: Still in re-/search. I think I might go with short or long based on company fundamentals and news coverage.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
That’s an interesting path — I’ve actually been down it before. I found a few strategies that work, for example scalping, but the problem is that fees eat everything. To stop fees from eating the edge you have to be a VIP client at Binance; then the conditions are completely different and the setup can work. Otherwise I don’t know how. So I really did find a few working strategies, but because my capital is limited I can’t become a VIP client. That’s why the whales are always ahead.  
As for what you said about company fundamentals — they get adjusted all the time, so it’s hard. You really have to look for something else, like momentum or similar approaches. Anyway, I won’t go into details — I have some ideas and that’s what I’m working on right now.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Posting a negative result with the always-up baseline and a random-entry comparison is exactly how it should be done. The baseline matters a lot, since a model that guesses up most of the time can look decent on direction alone. I'd also check whether the result changes in different periods, like rising years versus falling ones, in case a weak edge shows up in only one of them. It would be interesting to see if the same test gives a similar answer on a simple baseline model, to know how much of the miss is Granite and how much is the task being hard.
